evidence: Public header sparseSA.hpp: search() returns SA interval (count), SA/ISA are public members (locate), text retained. No documented end-user exact-search API or CLI; mummer prints MEMs only.
No IUPAC/wildcard/class patterns. Only a nucleotidesOnly flag (A/C/G/T mapped to 0-3 via BITADD table); non-ACGT simply breaks matches.
No k-mismatch/k-edit traversal of the index. nucmer extends exact MEM/MUM anchors with Smith-Waterman (sw_align.hh) between clustered anchors: seed-and-extend, not approximate index search.
Reference MEM/MUM engine: nucmer/mummer --mum, --mumreference, --maxmatch (all MEMs); 48-bit SA; human vs chimp aligned in 3h06m on 32 threads. repeat-match tool lists maximal repeats.
findMEM_each/findMUM_each/findMAM_each stream anchors of a query against the index via callback; queries processed one at a time. No ms[] array exposed (traverse/top_down primitives only).
sparseSAMatch indexes a multi-FASTA reference (descr_, startpos_) and from_set() maps hits to sequence id; nucmer handles many contigs. No k-common/LCS/document-listing API.
mummer -b and nucmer default use both strands (-f/-r restrict); only the query is reverse-complemented, coordinates documented (descending on reverse strand). Single flag, no manual RC.
Public suffixlink(), top_down(), top_down_child() (CHILD table), expand_link(), interval_t; LCP/ISA/SA public members. No tree/LCA API, almost no documentation.
Only CLI utilities repeat-match (maximal repeats) and exact-tandems; no LRS/distinct-substring/k-mer statistics API (LCP array public, so DIY).
SA built by libdivsufsort (replaced qsufsort), 'primarily single-threaded': ~36 min for 3 Gb human incl. ISA+LCP (~1.4 Mbp/s, 2012 Opteron). No head-to-head; libsais is 3-4x faster than divsufsort.
~15 B/base general, 13-14 B/base for large refs (6 B SA + 6 B ISA + 1 B LCP); human SA ~39 GB; human-chimp run peaked at 66 GB RAM. Sparse suffix sampling K can reduce.
No count/locate latency published. MEM throughput: nucmer4 ~10% faster than Bowtie2 and ~30% faster than BWA-MEM on 264M Illumina reads vs human; 45.1 GB RAM. Classed as SA+CHILD/suffix-link search.
48-bit offsets (limit 2^47-1, ~141 Tbp); human vs chimp (~3.1 vs 3.2 Gbp) aligned in 3h06m with up to 66 GB; MUMmer3 limit was ~500 Mb reference / ~4 Gb query; no query size cap in v4.
--batch X loads X reference bases at a time to fit RAM; SA can be saved/loaded (39 GB loads in ~3 min at 200 MB/s). Each batch index is still in RAM; no mmap/disk-resident search.
SA build is primarily single-threaded (OpenMP in SA build disabled in 4.0.0beta3). Threads work per query sequence: near-linear 2-16 thr, sublinear at 32; 3m43s vs 17m32s for nucmer3.
nucmer4 shares one read-only index among worker threads (one query sequence per thread); scaling to 32 threads documented; unittests/ include thread-pool and multi-thread tests.
Static index built once (or loaded); no append or insert/delete API in sparseSA.
No compressed index: plain 48-bit SA + ISA + LCP (13-15 B/base). Only sparse sampling (every K-th suffix, essaMEM lineage) trades size for query time; no published ratio.
Arbitrary characters (promer handles protein translations) plus nucleotidesOnly path mapping A/C/G/T to 0..3 (BITADD). No integer alphabets and no 2-bit packed text/SA.
Index save/load to files via prefix (4.0.0: save SA for reuse); 39 GB loads in ~3 min. Plain files: no mmap, no documented format versioning or integrity check.
C++17 library (pkg-config, SWIG bindings for Perl/Python/Ruby) and CLI tools; no C ABI. Best .NET routes: spawn nucmer/mummer CLI or write a C wrapper over C++ headers.
Bioconda (mummer4 4.0.1), Homebrew, GitHub release tarballs, Docker/Apptainer recipes; CLI suite (nucmer, mummer, dnadiff, show-*); SWIG bindings.
gtest unit tests (test_nucmer, test_sparse_sa, thread tests); make check + distcheck in GitHub Actions on Linux, FreeBSD, macOS; paper validates against MUMmer3 on real genomes.
Artistic-2.0 (OSI); 4.0.1 released 4 Feb 2025 (4.0.0 Jan 2021), CI on 3 OSes; ~161 open issues. Within 24 months of 2026-11-02 but no release since.
Construction libraries only (SA/GSA/BWT/LCP/PLCP): no query API. Contains/count/locate need user binary search over the SA plus own text access; no extract function.
No pattern matching of any kind; only suffix-sorting primitives.
No search functionality; approximate matching would have to be written from scratch (no Occ/rank structure, only raw SA, BWT, LCP arrays).
Supplies SA plus LCP/PLCP (also for GSA) primitives from which MEM/MUM/maximal repeats can be computed; no matching API, substantial user code needed.
No matching-statistics API; user can derive ms[] by binary search on the SA with own code. Library only provides construction primitives.
libsais_gsa (since 2.9.0) builds the generalized SA of 0-separated strings; libsais_plcp_gsa/lcp give GSA LCP. No k-common/LCS/document-listing API on top.
No reverse-complement or DNA awareness; user must index T + revcomp(T) as one string (or two SAs) and map strand/offsets.
Flat arrays only (SA, PLCP/LCP, BWT); no suffix links, LCP-interval tree, LCA; user must add RMQ/tree structures.
LCP/PLCP arrays enable LRS, distinct-substring counts etc. with a few lines of user code; no analytics API.
libsais 'dna' 404 MB: 4.98 s (81 MB/s) single-thread, 2.76 s (147 MB/s) 16 thr; divsufsort 19.2 s (21 MB/s). chr22 34.5 MB: 0.33 s vs 1.27 s. Fastest SACA in Rust crates benchmark too.
Plain uncompressed SA: 4n bytes (int32) / 8n (int64) + text (README: ~16 KB typical extra, worst case 2n; 5n for in-place BWT). 2 GB human: 8.0 GB peak (i32), 16.0 GB (i64).
No query API; exact count/locate = user binary search over SA, O(m log n) class. No latency numbers published.
libsais64/libsais16x64 use int64 offsets (inputs >=2 GB); Libsais64 built SA of first 2 GB of human genome in 78.5 s, 16.0 GB peak. libdivsufsort64 via BUILD_DIVSUFSORT64. No >=3 Gbp run shown.
All routines operate on caller RAM buffers (T, SA, fs workspace); no disk-based, semi-external or mmap mode.
libsais OpenMP: dna 404 MB 4.98 s -> 2.76 s on 16 thr (1.8x); enwik9 12.2 -> 7.9 s; skyline28 12.4 -> 3.4 s (3.7x). README: memory-bound, saturates near 8 threads. divsufsort MT ~1.2x.
No query structure; SA is a plain array safely shared read-only. Construction functions show no global state in headers, but thread-safety is not stated anywhere.
No online/dynamic operations; each call rebuilds from scratch.
Provides BWT (libsais_bwt, bwt_aux, cyclic) and inverse BWT as building blocks for FM/compressed indexes; no compressed index itself.
8-bit (libsais), 16-bit (libsais16), integer alphabets (libsais_int/_long with alphabet size k), 32- and 64-bit offsets; no 2-bit packed DNA path.
No serialization or file format; arrays are caller-owned memory.
C99 API with extern C linkage and plain pointers, CMake/CPM package: P/Invoke feasible, no managed wrapper; errors via int return codes (-1/-2); no spans.
GitHub source + CMake/CPM; third-party Rust crates libsais/libsais-sys; libdivsufsort in Debian (libdivsufsort-dev 2.0.1-6). No CLI, no PyPI/Conan/vcpkg/conda package found.
libsais repo root has no tests/ dir or CI workflows (include, src, Benchmarks.md, CHANGES, CMakeLists.txt); libdivsufsort CMake has no enable_testing. Trust rests on wide use.
libsais: Apache-2.0 w/ LLVM exception, v2.12.1 on 2026-10-21, ~10 releases since Jan 2025, 2 open issues. libdivsufsort: MIT but last release 2.0.1 in Nov 2010 (14 open issues).
Lookup(s,n) locates (unsorted; n<0 all), Bytes() gives text; no Count function (len of Lookup result) and no extract API. O(log N*len(s)+occ). int64 path beyond 2 GiB.

FindAllIndex(regexp) uses LiteralPrefix + Lookup, then anchored regex per candidate; classes/IUPAC via regexp syntax; with no literal prefix it falls back to a full scan. Prefix-accelerated post-filter.
API is only New, Lookup, FindAllIndex, Bytes, Read, Write; suffix array is unexported, so no approximate search and no way to backtrack over the index.
No MEM/MUM API and SA/LCP unexported. Only Lookup+Bytes: MEMs need O(m) Lookup probes plus own maximality checks; possible but slow, substantial user code.
No matching-statistics API; ms[i] derivable by repeated Lookup(prefix,1) extension (monotone trick), O(log N*len) per probe; user code required.
No multi-text API; user concatenates texts with separators and maps offsets to documents. No document listing, k-common or LCS support.
No reverse-complement or DNA awareness; user indexes T+revcomp(T) or queries both strands manually.
Index has only unexported fields; no suffix links, LCP, node or interval navigation exposed.
No analytics (LRS, distinct substrings, k-mer stats) and no SA/LCP access to build them.
SA-IS O(N) (since May 2019, 3-10x faster than qsufsort): 1M Go source 24.9 MB/s, 5M zeros 152 MB/s, 50M random 2.45 MB/s (32-bit, dev laptop). No DNA or head-to-head number.
About 5 B/char up to 2 GiB (1 text + 4 SA), about 9 B/char beyond (int64). SA-IS reuses the output buffer: 10M text alloc 80.2 MB -> 40.0 MB in the 2019 rewrite. Uncompressed.
Lookup is binary search over SA: O(log N*len(s)+len(result)) per docs; no published latency or throughput numbers.
int32 SA up to math.MaxInt32 bytes, int64 beyond (maxData32 switch); 64-bit path exercised by TestIndex64 on small data. No documented run at >=3 Gbp (would need ~27 GB).
New builds in RAM; Read loads the whole index into memory; no mmap or external-memory mode.
Single-threaded SA-IS construction; no parallel option in the API.
Lookup/FindAllIndex only read immutable fields, but neither docs nor source state thread-safety; concurrent use is by convention only.
Immutable index; no append, insert or delete.
Uncompressed SA (4-8 B/char in memory); Write only varint-encodes indices on disk. No compressed or succinct in-memory index.
Byte alphabet only ([]byte, 256 symbols); no integer or rune alphabet in the public API and no 2-bit DNA path (text_32/text_64 are internal).
Documented Write/Read (varint-chunked SA) with bounds validation returning errCorrupted; no mmap, no magic/version, no checksum.
Idiomatic Go ([]byte, io.Reader/Writer) but no C ABI; .NET use needs a custom cgo c-shared wrapper or sidecar process; no zero-copy into .NET.
Single channel: Go standard library, shipped in every Go toolchain and documented on pkg.go.dev. No CLI, no standalone package, no server surface.
Go CI tests with brute-force oracles (strings.Index, regexp), exhaustive binary inputs to length 21 and ternary to 14, 32/64-bit paths, corruption regressions. No fuzz tests.
BSD-3-Clause; ships with every Go release (go1.27.3, 2026-10-20). Core code unchanged since the May 2019 SA-IS rewrite except small cleanups (2022-2024); stable, low churn.
rust-bio FMIndex::backward_search gives SA interval in O(m) (count); locate via SuffixArray::get (raw or sampled). No text extract; sentinel needed, else silently wrong. fm-index: count+locate.
No pattern classes in FM/SA search. pattern_matching::myers supports ambiguous symbols and long patterns, and pssm scans motifs, but both scan text rather than an index.
No index-based approximate search. FMDIndex backward_ext/forward_ext bi-intervals allow DIY backtracking; myers (edit distance k) and ukkonen scan the text.
FMDIndex::smems/all_smems return supermaximal exact matches of a read on both strands (O(m), O(m^2)); no full MEM/MUM sets between genomes, no maximal repeated pairs.
smems(pattern,i,l)/all_smems give SMEM anchors; backward_search returns Partial (longest matching suffix). Matching-statistics-like per position, no ms[] array.
fm-index FMIndexMultiPieces: multi-text with PieceId per match (experimental, API may change); rust-bio allows multiple sentinels when concatenating. No k-common/LCS API.
FMDIndex (Li 2012) over T$R$: BiInterval yields forward() and revcomp() hits in one search. DNA+N alphabet only; user must build the T+revcomp text.
BiInterval/Interval with backward_ext/forward_ext (bidirectional navigation), LCP array (SmallInts), shortest_unique_substrings. No suffix links, LCA or tree visitors.
lcp() O(n), shortest_unique_substrings (Ohlebusch 2013), qgram_index; no LRS, distinct-substring count or supermaximal-repeat API.
rust-bio SAIS: first 2 GB of human genome in 957 s (2.1 MB/s) vs libsais 77 s and divsufsort 177 s, i.e. ~12x slower than libsais (laptop, shared benchmark by libsais crate author).
rust-bio SA build peaks at 23.9 GB for 2 GB text (~12 B/char; Vec<usize> SA plus workspace). Built FM-index smaller (Occ n/k*A words, sampled SA, plain-byte BWT); fm-index uses O(n log sigma) bits.
backward_search O(m) with Occ.get O(k) per step (k = sampling rate); fm-index uses wavelet matrix. No published latency/throughput for either crate.
usize (64-bit) offsets throughout; SA for 2 GB human built (23.9 GB peak, 957 s). No documented run at >=3 Gbp; fm-index offset width not documented.
All structures are in-memory (BWT Vec<u8>, Occ Vec<Vec<usize>>, sampled SA Vec<usize>); no mmap or disk-resident mode in rust-bio or fm-index.
SAIS and Occ construction are single-threaded; the shared benchmark lists no multithreaded bio entry (libsais OpenMP and psacak threads are other crates).
Query methods take &self over plain Vec fields without interior mutability, so indexes are Sync by Rust auto-traits; not explicitly documented or tested for concurrency.
Static indexes; only RankSelect gained push/extend (4.0.0). No online SA/FM updates.
fm-index: wavelet-matrix FM-index (O(n log sigma) bits) and RLFMIndex for repetitive texts; rust-bio: sampled Occ/SA but plain-byte BWT. No published ratio vs SA.
rust-bio: Alphabet over u8, suffix_array_int for integer alphabets, bitenc packing, DNA wavelet_matrix. fm-index: Character trait and Text::max_character set bits per symbol.
Occ derives serde Serialize/Deserialize and fm-index depends on serde, so indexes can be saved with a chosen serde format; no mmap, documented format, versioning or checksum.
Native Rust crates (slices, generics, typed errors) but no C ABI: .NET needs a custom cdylib wrapper; no managed binding.
crates.io + docs.rs only (bio ~1.18M downloads; fm-index ~100k). Library without CLI or server surface.
rust-bio CI (rust.yml, clippy) and Coveralls; FM tests assert hard-coded values, no brute-force oracle. fm-index has tests/ and benches/ dirs (contents not reviewed).
MIT (bio), MIT/Apache-2.0 (fm-index); bio 4.2.2 on 2026-10-12 with 4.0.0/4.1/4.2 releases in 2026, 67 open issues; fm-index 0.3.1 on 2026-06-29.
